history.heading: Penal colony and Pitcairners
paragraphs: Norfolk Island, in the South Pacific between Australia, New Zealand and New Caledonia, had been visited by Polynesians but was uninhabited when James Cook arrived in 1774. Britain established a penal settlement in 1788, and from 1825 to 1855 it was one of the harshest penal colonies in the British Empire. The Kingston and Arthur's Vale Historic Area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In 1856 the descendants of the Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions moved from overcrowded Pitcairn Island to Norfolk Island. Their arrival date, 8 June, is celebrated as Bounty Day.

culture.heading: Norf'k culture
paragraphs: English and Norf'k, a creole of 18th-century English and Tahitian, are official languages. About a third of residents descend from the Pitcairn settlers. The Norfolk Island pine is the island's symbol and appears on its flag.

politics.heading: Australian territory
paragraphs: Norfolk Island is an external territory of Australia. It had its own legislative assembly and considerable self-government from 1979, but Australia abolished it in 2015 and integrated the island into Australian systems, a move opposed by many residents, who have petitioned the UN. A regional council was later suspended, and the island is administered by Australian-appointed officials.

economy.heading: Tourism
paragraphs: Tourism, mainly from Australia and New Zealand, is the main industry. Residents now pay Australian taxes and receive Australian benefits since the 2016 reforms. The currency is the Australian dollar.
